prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its development into long-acting incretin therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My final position is a single-part B046 prize crediting Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, unchanged from round 1. The decisive point is that all six members agree on the science, its maturity and its independent confirmation, so the remaining question is only who takes the third place and how the citation is worded. Holst (incretin physiology and the active peptide forms) and Drucker (GLP-1 receptor and tissue biology, route to therapy) are named by all six of us. Knudsen's work on long-acting analogues is what turned the physiology into drugs with randomized benefit in glycaemia, weight, cardiovascular and renal endpoints. A citation that names both the physiology and its development into therapy describes the actual achievement, and three names fit the cap with no second part needed.
statement.case_against: The weakness is still attribution. Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1 peptide is a real contribution, the Habener group lies outside the supplied names, and none of us can verify the priority record from the material we are allowed to use. A reasonable committee could judge the discovery core to be Holst, Drucker and Mojsov and see Knudsen's inclusion as rewarding drug development over discovery. I have not found a reason in the round-1 exchange to think the priority record favours Mojsov decisively, but I also have no evidence that it does not, so my choice rests on how I weigh the translational half of the achievement, not on settled facts about priority.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius keeps Drucker, Holst and Mojsov as the discovery core, argues that three places cannot cover both discovery and drug development, and says that leaving out Knudsen risks a prize that stops short of the clinical achievement it cites.
responses.response: Her own reservation is close to mine, and it is the reason I do not move. She concedes that omitting Knudsen leaves the citation cut off from the medicines it invokes, and that including Mojsov carries attribution risk she has not verified. If I accept both of those statements, the Mojsov trio carries an unverified credit risk and an incomplete clinical half, while the Knudsen trio carries an unverified credit risk and a heavier development weighting. I think the second risk is easier to defend in a citation that says physiology and development explicitly. I would revisit if the committee can show from documents that Mojsov's peptide work was independent of the Habener group and necessary to the discovery; I do not have that record.

responses.point: Perlmann prefers a discovery-anchored citation with Mojsov, and says he would move toward the Knudsen trio if Mojsov's work cannot be separated from the Habener group or verified.
responses.response: His conditional is the right test, and on the evidence available to us it is not passed: nobody in round 1, Perlmann included, claims to have verified the separation. Without that, the Mojsov trio depends on a priority claim that the committee could be asked to defend and cannot. I also disagree that the anchoring in discovery needs Mojsov. Drucker and Holst already carry the physiology, so the open third place is the one where I think the drug-development contribution adds more to the citation than a third peptide-characterization credit would. I accept that this reflects weighting, and I would not call the Mojsov trio unreasonable.

responses.point: The chair asks whether a B046 citation should be discovery-led or discovery-to-therapy, and whether a second part should be added, noting he sees no clear gain from one.
responses.response: I support the discovery-to-therapy wording. The physiology is stated first and the development second, so it is not a drug-development prize, and it makes explicit that the Habener group and early peptide work sit outside the three credited names. On a second part, I agree there is no gain: B014 would add two people to three and break the cap of three in total, and a three-person B046 is already a complete prize. I keep B014 as my first alternative only for the case where B046 stalls on credit.

responses.point: El-Manira supports Drucker, Holst and Knudsen but says a reasonable committee could weigh the basic-science side more heavily, and notes that a very expected prize risks reading as a clinical-impact award.
responses.response: I agree with both points and treat them as the main cost of my choice. I would answer the second by keeping the citation anchored in physiology, with the therapies described as the development of that physiology, and by noting that GLP-1 passes the discovery test through Holst and Drucker independently of the drugs. Where I differ from him is that I would not accept a Mojsov-for-Knudsen swap on the unverified record alone; I would want the documents first, as I said in round 1.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can establish from documents that Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active peptide was independent of the Habener group; I cannot, and my position would change only if that were shown.
Whether the other members treat the physiology-and-development citation as discovery enough, or as weighted too far toward the industrial developer.

If B046 stalls, whether B014 (clean Walter and Mori credit, clinical consequence still prospective) or B037 (Eshhar's chimeric receptor concept outside the credited names) is the better stand-alone fallback; I lean to B014 on attribution.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. No conflict requiring recusal is apparent from my profile for B046, B014 or B037. I co-authored with Linnarsson and Frisen, who are colleagues and not credited names, and my field of RNA processing and single-cell methods is closest to B043, which is not in my configuration. I use only the round-1 and chair material and do not claim to have verified the priority record.
